Ileoanal pouch anastomosis allows for surgical re- moval of the colon without loss of continence or the need for an ostomy, but subsequent inflammation of the pouch (pouchitis) occurs in about half of all pa- tients.4 On the basis of limited evidence it is consid- ered to be best treated by a short course of antibacte- rials (metronidazole or ciprofloxacin).3,4 If these are ineffective, mesalazine or corticosteroids may be considered.3 Use of a probiotic formulation, VSL-3, containing a mixture of bacteria, may also be of ben- efit.3,4 Crohn’s disease. • ACTIVE DISEASE: • mild to moderate First-line therapy in mild to moderate Crohn’s disease is a matter of some debate. Oral mesalazine is of lim- ited benefit in ileal or ileocaecal disease,5,6 and some consider that it should not be used at all,6 although others recommend high doses as an appropriate initial therapy.3 Aminosalicylates may be of more benefit in colonic disease, particularly sulfasalazine if it can be tolerated.3,5,6 Others favour the use of oral budeso- nide as first-line therapy for mild to moderate ileocae- cal disease;5,6 although it is somewhat less effective than conventional oral corticosteroids, which are an option in more active disease,3,5 it produces fewer ad- verse effects. Opinion also varies on the use of topical mesalazine in colonic disease,3,5 although it is widely used.5 Nutritional support (enteral feeding or the use of elemental diets) may be considered as an alterna- tive to drug therapy or surgery in selected patients.3 • moderate to severe In outpatients with moderate to severe disease, and those who fail to respond to initial therapy with budesonide or aminosalicylates, conventional oral corticosteroids, typically in a dose corresponding to 40 mg of prednisolone daily (or up to 1 mg/kg daily), are recommended.3,5,6 Once response has been achieved, dosage should be gradually tapered off.3,5 In patients who have relapsed, azathioprine or mer- captopurine may be added,5 but they are not best suit- ed to induction of remission because of the delay in onset.6 Methotrexate may be an alternative in selected patients.5 In patients with severe extensive or fulminant disease intravenous corticosteroids should be given.3,5,6 Add- ing intravenous metronidazole may be advisable, be- cause of the difficulty of distinguishing active disease from a septic complication.3 Infliximab should be considered in patients with disease refractory to cor- ticosteroids;3,5,6 adalimumab or certolizumab pegol may be alternatives.6 • fis
